snippet.title: This Fixes 95% of Posture Problems (FAST!)
snippet.description:
If you want to learn how to fix bad posture in 22 days, this step by step video gives you a plan for improving posture with stretches and strengthening exercises. Instead of guessing which posture exercises you need, I’m going to show you six simple tests you can perform at home to identify areas that need attention. Then, I’ll show you the stretches and exercises to address them and build your own posture correction routine.

Workouts, supplements, and mealplans here - http://athleanx.com
Subscribe to this channel here - http://youtube.com/user/jdcav24

The key to better posture is addressing your specific limitations consistently. This 22 day posture routine starts with testing your movement so you can focus on the areas that need work.

How to fix bad posture:

Day one starts with the posture test. As a physical therapist, I recommend seeing a qualified professional for an individual evaluation to understand your posture, the severity of any limitations and differences between your left and right sides. The six tests in this video give you a starting point for identifying areas to work on at home.

We’re looking at six areas: thoracic spine mobility, hamstring flexibility, calf flexibility, abdominal flexibility, hip flexor mobility and hip rotation. A rounded upper back, tight hamstrings, tight calves, tight abs, tight hip flexors and limited hip rotation can all affect how you move. Testing each area helps you decide which mobility exercises and stretches belong in your routine.

Each test uses a pass or fail approach. If you pass a test, you can skip the corresponding correction in this plan. If you fail a test, include the stretches and strengthening exercises shown for that area. This keeps your posture workout focused on your results instead of having you perform every exercise whether you need it or not.

After your initial assessment, alternate stretching days with exercise or strengthening days for the next 20 days. Follow the recommended hold times, sets and reps demonstrated in the video for each of your selected corrections. On day 22, repeat the original tests to see where your mobility and control have improved and what still needs attention.

For example, if your upper back is rounded and you struggle to extend through your thoracic spine, start with the kneeling thoracic extension stretch. Place your elbows on a surface in front of you, lower your chest and gently move your upper back into extension. The goal is to work on upper back mobility with control rather than force yourself into a position you cannot comfortably reach.

On your strengthening days, the face pull works the muscles of the upper back and shoulders. When you’re looking for exercises for rounded shoulders or ways to improve upper body posture, it’s easy to focus only on stretching. This routine pairs mobility work with strengthening so you also train the muscles that help you control your position.

The same approach applies to the other areas you test. Tight hip flexors, limited hip rotation or tight hamstrings may call for different corrections, which is why the assessment comes first. Use the demonstrations to choose your exercises for bad posture, and follow the instructions instead of adding random stretches to your day.

Improving posture takes consistency. You didn’t develop your everyday movement habits in a single day, and one posture stretch is not going to change everything overnight. Treat these 22 days as an opportunity to establish a repeatable routine, measure your progress and learn which areas deserve more attention.

You also don’t want to overdo the stretching. More force does not automatically mean better flexibility. Stay within a comfortable range, use controlled movement and avoid pushing through pain. The goal of these stretches for better posture is to gradually improve the movement you have available, not turn each session into a test of how much discomfort you can tolerate.

A useful posture correction routine combines flexibility, joint mobility and strength. Stretching addresses the restrictions identified by your tests, while the strengthening days help you practice controlling your movement. Keep following the schedule and use your final assessment to guide what you continue working on beyond day 22.

If you want to support better posture over the long term, complement this routine with a workout program that strengthens your entire body. The ATHLEAN-X programs combine strength training with attention to how you move. Head to athleanx.com and use the program selector to find the training plan that fits your goals.

snippet.title: Best Home Ab Workout // Just 10 Min // 6 PACK GUARANTEED!
snippet.description:
If you are looking for the best home ab workout you can do without any equipment, this 10 minute follow along routine is a great place to start. In this video, I’m going to take you through seven bodyweight ab exercises that you can do in the comfort of your own home, whether you are a beginner or an experienced lifter.

Get a flat stomach here - https://athleanx.com/flatstomach
Subscribe to this channel here - http://bit.ly/2b0coMW

The key to a successful home abs workout is keeping it simple enough to do consistently while making sure the exercises challenge your core. You don’t need an ab machine, a set of dumbbells or a gym membership. Every exercise in this routine uses your own bodyweight, and all you need is enough floor space to move comfortably.

The structure of the ab workout is simple.

There are 7 exercises, each performed for 60 seconds. If you are a beginner and cannot make it through the entire minute, perform the exercise for as long as you can with good form. Take a brief break when needed and rejoin the workout when you are ready. Your goal is to gradually build up the strength and endurance to complete more of each interval without sacrificing the quality of your reps.

Some of the exercises are divided into 30 seconds on each side or in each direction. These changes are noted below and demonstrated in the video so you can follow along without stopping to figure out what comes next.

Between exercises, you will get 30 seconds to rest. During that time, I’ll explain the next movement and show you how to perform it. This makes the routine easy to save and come back to whenever you want an ab workout at home that takes the guesswork out of your training.

Here is how the workout breaks down:

1. Ab Halos - 30 seconds clockwise / 30 seconds counterclockwise | 30 seconds rest
2. Frog Crunches - 60 seconds | 30 seconds rest
3. Russian Rows - 60 seconds | 30 seconds rest
4. Thread the Needle - 30 seconds each side | 30 seconds rest
5. Black Widow Knee Slides - 60 seconds | 30 seconds rest
6. Frog Circles - 60 seconds | 30 seconds rest
7. Sliding Ab Tucks - 60 seconds

Remember, the goal is not to rush through as many reps as possible just to keep moving for the full minute. Focus on controlling each rep and making your abs do the work. A shorter interval performed well gives you a better starting point than forcing yourself through an exercise after you have lost control of the movement.

What makes this home ab workout effective is the variety of ways you are challenging your core. Instead of repeating the same crunch over and over, you will work through movements that involve curling, rotation and maintaining control of your trunk as your arms and legs move. Pay attention to the demonstrations so you understand what each exercise should look like before your next interval begins.

One of the problems with many ab workouts is that people focus on moving their legs without paying attention to what their pelvis and lower back are doing. Your hip flexors naturally contribute to certain movements, but simply swinging your legs through a rep is not the same thing as deliberately training your abs.

Watch the position of your body, control the movement and follow the form cues throughout the video. If you can no longer maintain that control, pause and reset. Don’t assume that making an exercise faster or forcing a bigger range of motion will make it a better ab exercise.

People often ask how often they should train their abs. The first step is finding a routine you can perform consistently and recover from. Having a short, no equipment ab workout ready to go makes that easier. You can fit it around your regular workouts or do it at home when getting to the gym is not an option.

As you improve, use the same routine to measure your progress. Can you complete more of the interval with clean reps? Can you take fewer breaks without rushing? Can you maintain better control from the first exercise to the last? Those are useful signs that your core strength and endurance are improving.

Of course, building your abs and revealing your abs are two parts of the same goal. This workout can help you train your abdominal muscles, but getting visible six pack abs also depends on your overall body fat levels. Pair your training with a consistent approach to nutrition instead of expecting an ab workout alone to reveal your six pack.

snippet.title: The ONLY 2 DB Biceps Exercises You Need (NO, SERIOUSLY!)
snippet.description:
Get big biceps here - https://athleanx.com
Subscribe to the ATHLEAN-X channel here - http://bit.ly/2b0coMW

What if I told you that here were only 2 dumbbell biceps exercises you need to grow bigger biceps, would you believe me? In this video, I am going to show you how only two dumbbell biceps exercises are all that is required to build big biceps. Remember, it comes down to not only the choice of the exercise you make, but how do them that makes all the difference.

The first exercise out of the only 2 dumbbell biceps exercises you need to build bigger biceps is a variation of an already popular biceps exercise. You might have seen or you are already doing the incline curl, but there is a better way to do it that will help you to build bigger biceps. Instead of performing the standard incline curl, I want you to do an incline drag curl to target the long head of the biceps.

This exercise combines the benefits of the incline curl and the drag curl while keeping the limitations of the incline curl out of the equation. It starts, however, with the incline position of the bench. You want to aim for about 60 degrees as too far upright will eliminate the stretch you get on the biceps at the bottom of the range of motion. A lesser incline, say 45-30 degrees, will allow you to get a stretch on the biceps, but to a degree that will likely cause discomfort on the biceps tendon and the anterior shoulder structure.

You are going to want to use light weight when performing this dumbbell biceps exercise as it will be all you can really handle. The key here is to eliminate the momentum you might be using on the incline curl and eliminate over activation of the front delt as you swing the dumbbells in order to move the weight. Shoulder flexion does come into play, but a little later in the range of motion of the incline drag curl. So, keep your elbows in place as you curl the weight up, essentially dragging the dumbbell straight up as you curl. At the top of the range of motion, you are going to want to supinate the dumbbells as much as you can while you get a small amount of shoulder flexion as we know to get bigger biceps, you want to activate all 3 functions of the biceps to get a complete contraction of the biceps muscles: elbow flexion, supination, and shoulder flexion.

The second exercise of the only 2 dumbbell bicep exercises you need is one you are probably already doing, but, there is a possibility you are doing it wrong. First, it's important to note why the dumbbell preacher curl is the perfect compliment to the incline drag curl we already discussed. If the drag curl is targeting the long head of the biceps, especially on stretch, then we need to next try to influence the biceps short head and peak contraction. The other great part is that this preacher curl can be done with the exact same setup as the incline drag curl.

The preacher curl is immensely popular, but there is a right way and a wrong way of performing the exercise that will either prevent or lead to a biceps tendon tear. If you keep the same bench setup as the incline curl, you are already headed in the right direction. You see, too steep of an incline on the bench or preacher pad and not standing over it is going to lead to a lot of stress on the biceps tendon.

Instead, when you perform the preacher curl, you want to stand over the incline of the bench where your triceps stay flush with the bench at all times win the range of motion. This will allow you to use your lats to assist in the movement and protect your biceps in the process. As you curl the dumbbell, you want to dig your elbow and triceps into the bench, almost trying to pull it towards yourself as you curl. This will take the biceps out of a vulnerable position and allow you to curl the weight without risk.

With your arm more out in front of you, you are already getting the necessary shoulder flexion that influences the biceps contraction. On top of that, the elbow flexion (curl) and forced supination will lead to greater biceps growth.

With those two dumbbell biceps exercises, you are training the biceps through stretch and peak contraction - covering the whole range of motion of the biceps in order to build bigger biceps.

snippet.title: Give Me 2 Dumbbells... I'll Build You a BIGGER Chest
snippet.description:
Build a Big Chest Here - https://athleanx.com
Subscribe to This Channel Here - http://bit.ly/2b0coMW

If you want to learn how to build a big chest with dumbbells only, then you’ve come to the right video. I’m going to show you how to build your upper chest, develop your lower pecs, and get a stronger contraction through the middle of your chest with 8 chest workout techniques. Whether you do your chest workouts at home or in the gym, these tips will help you get more out of the dumbbell chest exercises you’re already doing.

It starts with a couple of mechanical keys that you want to make sure you’re still taking advantage of when you perform chest exercises with dumbbells. The first is leg drive on the dumbbell bench press. As you press the dumbbells away from your chest at the bottom of the rep, think about pushing your feet into the floor as if you were trying to slide your body up the bench. Get your feet set before you start pressing so you can use that drive from the very first rep.

Keep in mind, this is easier to feel when you use heavier dumbbells. The weight helps keep your shoulders pinned to the bench and prevents your body from actually sliding. You want to feel how pushing through your feet gives you a more stable base to press from, especially as you try to get the dumbbells moving at the bottom.

The next thing you want to take advantage of is the freedom you have to move each dumbbell independently. When you bench press with a barbell, your hands are fixed to the bar for the entire rep. With dumbbells, you can tilt your thumbs up slightly as you press, allowing you to bring the weights closer together at the top. Pay attention to what happens to your upper arms. Bringing them toward each other is called adduction, and it’s what helps you get a better contraction of the pecs on this chest exercise.

Next, you want to explore the underhand dumbbell bench press. This is one of my favorite dumbbell exercises for chest development if you train at home and don’t have access to an incline bench. Flipping your grip helps you engage your lats as you set up to press. It also changes the path of the dumbbells. You’re pressing from low and away to up and in, which gives you a way to target the upper chest fibers while keeping the bench flat.

From here, you want to be sure you’re including drop sets in your dumbbell chest workout. The best part is that you can do one even if you only have a single pair of dumbbells. Immediately after finishing a heavy set of dumbbell bench presses, set the weights down, drop to the floor, and perform pushups to failure. Your pecs are already fatigued from pressing, so you can keep working them with your own bodyweight.

Next, the static dumbbell bench press is another way to challenge your chest without needing a heavy barbell. Hold one dumbbell steady while you press with the opposite arm, then switch sides. This is a great way to expose a difference in strength or control that you may overlook when both arms press together. Where you hold the stationary dumbbell makes a difference, too. For an even greater challenge, try holding it down near your chest while the other arm completes its reps.

Finally, there are three dumbbell chest exercises you want to make sure you’re not overlooking. The first is the dumbbell pullover. If you flare your elbows out to the sides and think about pulling with them, you’re going to feel your lats doing more of the work. To get more out of the pullover for your chest, think about squeezing your hands together against the dumbbell as you bring it back over you.

The UCV dumbbell raise gives you a way to bring your upper arm farther across your chest than you can on a press. That extra adduction at the top of the rep is what makes this such a good dumbbell chest exercise for getting a more complete pec contraction. Keep in mind, you’ll want to use a lighter weight here so you can control that path all the way across your body.

Finally, the dumbbell chest fly gives you a chance to overload adduction and take advantage of the eccentric, or lowering, portion of the rep. Perform the fly on the floor and slow the dumbbells down as you lower them. The floor gives your upper arms a stopping point on each rep, which is particularly helpful as you progress to heavier dumbbells.

With dumbbells, you can tilt your thumbs up slightly as you press, allowing you to bring the weights closer together at the top. Pay attention to what happens to your upper arms. Bringing them toward each other is called adduction, and it’s what helps you get a better contraction of the pecs on this chest exercise.

Next, you want to explore the underhand dumbbell bench press. This is one of my favorite dumbbell exercises for chest development if you train at home and don’t have access to an incline bench. Flipping your grip helps you engage your lats as you set up to press. It also changes the path of the dumbbells. You’re pressing from low and away to up and in, which gives you a way to target the upper chest fibers while keeping the bench flat.

From here, you want to be sure you’re including drop sets in your dumbbell chest workout. The best part is that you can do one even if you only have a single pair of dumbbells. Immediately after finishing a heavy set of dumbbell bench presses, set the weights down, drop to the floor, and perform pushups to failure. Your pecs are already fatigued from pressing, so you can keep working them with your own bodyweight.

Next, the static dumbbell bench press is another way to challenge your chest without needing a heavy barbell. Hold one dumbbell steady while you press with the opposite arm, then switch sides. This is a great way to expose a difference in strength or control that you may overlook when both arms press together. Where you hold the stationary dumbbell makes a difference, too. For an even greater challenge, try holding it down near your chest while the other arm completes its reps.

Finally, there are three dumbbell chest exercises you want to make sure you’re not overlooking. The first is the dumbbell pullover. If you flare your elbows out to the sides and think about pulling with them, you’re going to feel your lats doing more of the work. To get more out of the pullover for your chest, think about squeezing your hands together against the dumbbell as you bring it back over you.

The UCV dumbbell raise gives you a way to bring your upper arm farther across your chest than you can on a press. That extra adduction at the top of the rep is what makes this such a good dumbbell chest exercise for getting a more complete pec contraction. Keep in mind, you’ll want to use a lighter weight here so you can control that path all the way across your body.

Finally, the dumbbell chest fly gives you a chance to overload adduction and take advantage of the eccentric, or lowering, portion of the rep. Perform the fly on the floor and slow the dumbbells down as you lower them. The floor gives your upper arms a stopping point on each rep, which is particularly helpful as you progress to heavier dumbbells.

snippet.title: It's Weird, But it Drops Body Fat Faster Than Dieting!
snippet.description:
Want to lose weight without counting calories, tracking macros, or weighing every bite of food? You can. In this video, I’m showing you a simple, visual way to eat for fat loss using the food already on your plate. No calorie-counting app, complicated diet rules, or endless food math required.

Subscribe to this channel here - http://bit.ly/2b0coMW

Here’s the truth: calories still matter. If your goal is to lose body fat, your overall calorie intake has to support that goal. But that does NOT mean you have to spend your day adding up numbers to make progress. The easier you can make your nutrition plan to follow, the better your chances of sticking with it long enough to get results—and KEEP them.

I’m Jeff Cavaliere, physical therapist and strength coach, and I want to show you the plate method I still use myself. If you’re wondering how to lose weight without counting calories, you can try it at your very next meal.

FREE CARBOHYDRATE FOOD LISTS:
https://athleanx.com/carbs

First, look at your dinner plate and divide it visually into three equal sections. Dedicate one-third to PROTEIN: chicken, steak, fish, or another protein source you enjoy. Vegetarian or vegan? You can use plant-based options such as lentils, chickpeas, and other foods that fit the way you eat.

Now look at the remaining two-thirds. This is where your carbohydrate choices make a difference. I divide them into two categories: fibrous carbs and starchy carbs.

FIBROUS CARBOHYDRATES include broccoli, carrots, onions, mushrooms, and other vegetables you actually like. These foods typically provide more volume for fewer calories and help make your meals filling.

STARCHY CARBOHYDRATES include sweet potatoes, pasta, and similar foods. You do NOT have to eliminate them to lose fat. They’re especially valuable when you train hard and need fuel for your workouts.

If your main priority is losing a significant amount of body fat, give more of the remaining plate space to fibrous vegetables and a smaller section to starchy carbohydrates. You can still enjoy potatoes and pasta; you’re simply controlling the proportions visually instead of calculating every calorie.

If you're training consistently and need more fuel for performance, reverse that balance: more room for starches and less for vegetables, while keeping your protein section. I’ll show you how I put together a meal with chicken, sweet potatoes, pasta, and edamame to support my own training.

What about FATS? They’re included in how you prepare the meal: olive oil for sautéing vegetables, the fat in your protein preparation, or a reasonable amount of butter on a sweet potato. Just be mindful of how much you add. Oils and butter still contribute calories, even when you’re not counting them.

There’s also one mistake that can undermine this entire approach: PILING YOUR FOOD TOO HIGH.

One-third of a plate doesn’t mean a six-inch mountain of food. Look at your plate from the SIDE as well as from above. That second view helps you judge portion sizes, not just the surface area each food occupies. If you’re trying to lose weight without tracking every serving, this matters.

What if your weight loss stalls? You don't need to cut out all carbs or abandon the plan. Start by shifting some of the starchy portion toward fibrous vegetables. If you still need to adjust, give a little more room to satiating protein while slightly reducing the carbohydrate portion. These are small, repeatable changes—not an extreme diet overhaul.

The best fat loss diet is one you can stick with. Tracking calories can help, but using a food scale, calorie calculator, and daily tally for every meal gets exhausting. It’s not the only way to manage energy intake.

IN THIS VIDEO, YOU’LL LEARN:
• How to portion your plate for weight loss without counting calories
• Why protein comes first when planning a meal
• How fibrous carbs differ from starchy carbohydrates
• How to adjust carbohydrates for fat loss or athletic performance
• Why food portion HEIGHT matters, not just plate space
• What to change when your weight loss progress slows

This isn’t a magic belly fat-burning food list or a metabolism hack. Nor am I saying that a calorie deficit doesn’t matter. I’m showing you a straightforward system that can help you manage calories WITHOUT constantly thinking about calories. You make better food choices, monitor your progress, and adjust your portions when necessary.

https://athleanx.com/carbs

https://athleanx.com

snippet.title: Please STOP Gripping Your Dumbbells Like This!
snippet.description:
If your wrists hurt when you dumbbell bench press, take a closer look at how you are holding the weights. A small change in your grip may help make this chest exercise more comfortable without completely changing the way you press. In this video, I show you a dumbbell bench press tip that shifts the focus from how much weight you can lift to how your wrists feel while you lift it.

Train Smarter Here - https://athleanx.com
Subscribe to This Channel Here - http://bit.ly/2b0coMW

First, look at your current dumbbell bench press form. Watch the clips in this video and compare them to how you hold your dumbbells, especially at the top of each rep. Are you forcing both ends of the dumbbell to stay perfectly level with the floor? Or do you allow a slight tilt, with your thumb sitting a little higher than your pinky?

The goal here is to find a comfortable, controlled grip that lets you train your chest without your wrists becoming the limiting factor. If every set is interrupted by wrist discomfort, adding more weight is not the answer. Before you worry about progressing your dumbbell bench press, pay attention to where the handle sits in your hand and whether your wrist position changes as you press.

The adjustment shown starts with moving your hand slightly toward the thumb side of the dumbbell handle. Instead of insisting that the dumbbell remain perfectly horizontal, allow the pinky side to sit slightly lower. Watch the demonstration closely. This is a small adjustment in how you hold and balance the weight, not a cue to force your wrist into an exaggerated angle.

Why might this help? The position of the dumbbell in your hand changes how the load is supported at your wrist. A grip that looks symmetrical does not automatically feel comfortable for every person. The video explains the wrist positioning using the radius and ulna, the two bones of the forearm. The practical takeaway is to evaluate whether a subtle change in grip reduces the pinching or pressure you notice during the exercise.

That does not mean every case of wrist pain comes from the same problem, or that one grip adjustment will fix every painful wrist. It means your dumbbell grip is worth checking. Use a light pair of dumbbells to compare the positions shown so that you can focus on control and comfort.

There is another detail to pay attention to: how you squeeze the handle. In the demonstration, the emphasis shifts toward the thumb and index finger. Keep the remaining fingers wrapped securely around the dumbbell for stability. This is not a reason to loosen your hand or let the dumbbell move around during the set.

Think of this as a cue to make your grip more deliberate. Rather than simply grabbing the dumbbells and starting your reps, take a moment to establish the position before you press. Notice where the handle rests, how the dumbbell balances and whether you can maintain that setup throughout the movement. Your grip should feel secure at the bottom, through the press and at the top.

Keep the purpose of the adjustment in mind. We are trying to make the dumbbell bench press more comfortable for your wrists so you can focus on training your chest. You do not need to turn this into a test of how much more weight you can lift. If the lighter dumbbells feel better, practice the setup and make sure the same comfort and control carry over from rep to rep.

Also, do not confuse the slight tilt shown here with allowing the weight to fold your wrist backward. Pay attention to the full demonstration rather than copying only the appearance of the dumbbells at lockout. A useful technique change is one you can control throughout the set, without creating a new uncomfortable position elsewhere.

If you have been searching for how to stop wrist pain during dumbbell bench press, start by watching your grip as closely as you watch your pressing technique. This small detail may be the adjustment that helps you perform the exercise more comfortably. If the change hurts, stop. Persistent or worsening wrist pain deserves an assessment rather than repeated attempts to push through it.

Try the grip adjustment shown in your next chest workout with a light weight and see how your wrists respond. The priority is a secure grip, controlled reps and a chest exercise that feels comfortable.

snippet.title: The ONLY 2 Dumbbell Triceps Exercises You Need (NO, SERIOUSLY!)
snippet.description:
Get big triceps here - https://athleanx.com
Subscribe to the channel here - http://bit.ly/2b0coMW

What if I told you that here were only 2 dumbbell triceps exercises you need to grow bigger triceps, would you believe me? In this video, I am going to show you how only two dumbbell triceps exercises are all that is required to build big triceps. Remember, it comes down to not only the choice of the exercise you make, but how do them that makes all the difference.

The first exercise out of the only 2 dumbbell triceps exercises you need to build bigger triceps is a variation of an already popular triceps exercise. You might recognize this exercise as the dumbbell overhead triceps extension where you stand in space and hold a single dumbbell behind your head with both hands. This is a great exercise for targeting the long head of the triceps - the head of the muscle that makes up the most size of the triceps.

However, for many with limited shoulder mobility, it causes shoulder discomfort with the arms up overhead and with hands back behind the head. This can be fixed by making one big alteration to the exercise; using an incline bench.

By leaning back against an incline bench, you provide your shoulders with a much more comfortable position where your arms are not directly overhead, but rather slightly in front of you. This eliminates the shoulder discomfort but allows for enough stretch on the long head of the triceps that you will still see the benefits of the exercise. This more natural, comfortable position will also allow you to keep your elbows pointing straight forward instead of flaring them. This means that you are remaining in the scapular plane and are preventing internal rotation of the shoulder joint with elevation.

There is also an added safety factor to this version of the exercise outside of the shoulder positioning that will allow you to keep building big triceps as time goes on. The incline version of this exercise allows for enough clearance so that you don't ever hit your head with the dumbbell at any point in the range of motion. Add in that once you reach failure, you don't have to worry about dropping the dumbbell. Instead, simply slide down the bench and allow the dumbbell to catch itself on the top of the bench where you will easily be able to manipulate the dumbbell in space, safely.

The second exercise of the only 2 dumbbell tricep exercises you need is one you might have stopped doing a long time ago: the tricep kickback. The kickback gets a bad rap from many online influencers and keyboard scientists arguing that active insufficiency makes the exercise worthless. Basically, they are saying that you are actively minimizing the amount of force the triceps can produce and thus you must subjugate yourself to light weights that won't build muscle.

If active insufficiency was a real problem, then we should be avoiding exercises like leg extensions and preacher curls because they don't allow you to lift as much weight as a barbell squat or curl. The argument against the kickback is flawed because muscles don't know what weight is measured on the side of the dumbbell, but instead respond to overall tension. If the triceps are subjected to high tension due to muscle length shortening plus the weight of the dumbbell, we still have an opportunity to build muscle.

The kickback works as perfect compliment to the incline powerbomb because while we have trained the triceps with the long head on stretch, we need an exercise that trains the triceps with the long head in it's most shortened / contracted position. This requires getting the elbow and shoulder into extension (meaning your arm goes back behind your body).

We are going to utilize the incline bench once again, but this time, we are going to lower the incline to about 30 degrees. This is the perfect position to assume the proper posture and arm position required to make the kickback as effective as possible. This incline will allow for your triceps to be perfectly parallel with the floor when you reach the top end of the range of motion.

Hold the rep at the top for a second or two and realize exactly what you've been missing by skipping this incredible triceps exercise.

With those two exercise, you are training the long head of the triceps on stretch and in peak contraction - covering the whole range of motion of the triceps in order to build bigger triceps.

snippet.title: It's Extreme, But I'll NEVER Eat These 7 Foods Again!
snippet.description:
Eat like an athlete here - https://athleanx.com
Subscribe - http://bit.ly/2b0coMW

Trying to eat healthier in 2026? Before you overhaul your diet, take a closer look at the foods you already consider healthy. In this video, I break down 7 foods and food choices I'm reconsidering, from bananas in smoothies and whole grain bread to canned soup, artificial food dyes, farm-raised salmon and yogurt. Some are personal preferences. Others raise questions about ingredients, processing and whether you're getting the benefits you expect.

Whether you want to lose body fat or build muscle, a healthy diet goes beyond counting calories. I'll explain my reasoning and what to look for when choosing foods.

First up: bananas. Are bananas bad for you? Do bananas make you fat? Bananas can fit into a balanced diet and a fat loss meal plan. The issue discussed here is what happens when you blend them into a smoothie alongside certain beneficial plant compounds.

A 2023 study investigated how polyphenol oxidase, an enzyme abundant in bananas, affects the availability of flavanols in smoothies. Under the conditions tested, the banana smoothie substantially reduced the measured availability of these compounds compared with the control. That is more specific than saying bananas destroy every antioxidant in your shake. If you're choosing smoothie ingredients to maximize flavanol intake, this research gives you something to consider. Eating a banana separately is a different question.

Next, we look at whole grain bread and comments from Dr. Robert Lustig about food processing. Terms such as "multigrain" and "made with whole grains" can make a loaf sound healthier without telling you how much whole grain it contains. Check the ingredient list, fiber content, added sugar and serving size instead of relying on the front of the package.

Grinding a grain into flour does not automatically stop it from being whole grain. However, the structure and processing of a food can influence how it is digested. The takeaway is to compare breads carefully and choose options that support your nutrition goals. Bread doesn't have to disappear from your diet to get lean.

Then comes white bean soup and a personal experience I won't forget. After eating it shortly before a severe gastrointestinal illness, I developed an aversion that still makes it difficult to enjoy. That explains my decision, but it doesn't make white beans a bad food. It also opens a discussion about soup labels.

With canned soup, pay attention to sodium and the number of servings per container. If the nutrition information is listed for one serving and you eat two, your actual intake is twice the listed amount. snippet.title: I'm 51. This is What I Eat EVERY Day to Be Lean.
snippet.description:
Want to know what to eat to get shredded, build muscle, and stay lean all year? In this video, I’m sharing 12 foods I eat every day that make my diet easier to follow and help me maintain six pack abs without giving up the foods I enjoy.

Get Lean and Stay Lean Here - https://athleanx.com
Subscribe to this channel here - http://bit.ly/2b0coMW

If you’ve been looking for the Jeff Cavaliere diet plan or wondering how to eat like ATHLEAN-X, this is a look at the foods behind my daily eating plan. I’ll explain what I eat, why I choose it, and how these foods fit into a muscle building diet that supports hard training while keeping calories under control.

Getting lean takes more than finding the right foods. Your total calories, protein intake, workouts, and consistency all matter. But choosing meals that satisfy your appetite and taste good makes it easier to stick with your nutrition plan long enough to see results.

Here are some of the foods I rely on every day.

My breakfast starts with egg whites. They give me a convenient source of protein without adding many calories or much fat. When your goal is to get ripped while maintaining muscle, having an easy way to include protein at breakfast helps you start the day on track. Egg whites also leave room for other foods in the meal without making it difficult to manage your overall calorie intake.

Oatmeal is another staple of my daily meal plan. It provides carbohydrates to fuel my workouts, along with fiber that helps make breakfast more satisfying. I use plain oatmeal so I can control what goes into it instead of relying on varieties with added sugar. If you’re wondering what to eat to be lean, a breakfast you enjoy and can prepare consistently is a great place to start.

I drink skim milk with breakfast and use it in my oatmeal and protein shake later in the day. It supplies protein and calcium while keeping calories lower than the same amount of whole milk. Because I consume it several times throughout the day, that difference helps me keep my diet aligned with my goals. I also choose milk fortified with vitamins A and D.

Cinnamon is a simple addition that makes my oatmeal taste better without needing a lot of added sugar. That matters because a diet for abs should include meals you look forward to eating. Small choices that improve flavor can make a healthy eating plan easier to repeat, and repetition is a big part of staying lean year-round.

Greek yogurt is one of my go-to lunch foods because it’s convenient, versatile, and high in protein. It already contains all nine essential amino acids, making it a complete protein source. I like adding chia or pumpkin seeds for extra texture and nutrients. Pay attention to the variety you choose, since protein, calories, and added sugar can vary between products.

I’ve said plenty of times that I have a sweet tooth. Instead of expecting that to disappear, I make room for a dessert I enjoy. For me, that means a portion of frozen yogurt that fits my daily calorie intake. The amount and toppings matter. Having six pack abs doesn’t require eliminating dessert, but it does require being aware of how those choices fit into your overall diet.

Chicken, fish, and lean cuts of red meat are regular parts of my eating plan. I typically build my main meals around a serving that provides approximately 30–50 grams of protein. Getting enough protein helps support muscle growth and maintenance, making it a priority whether I’m focused on building muscle or staying lean. Different seasonings and preparation methods keep these meals from becoming repetitive.

Yes, I eat pasta. Carbohydrates have a place in a meal plan to get ripped, especially when you’re training hard and want to support your performance. Pasta gives me a food I enjoy and a practical source of workout fuel. Portion size and what you add to it matter. I make it fit my nutrition goals instead of assuming I need to cut it out to get a six pack.

Vegetables like broccoli help round out my meals with fiber, vitamins, and minerals. They also add volume to my plate, which can make a meal more satisfying when I’m managing calories. A muscle building nutrition plan needs to support more than your protein target, and vegetables are a consistent part of how I do that.

Watch the full video for all 12 foods and the reasons I include them in my daily diet.

Whether you want to build muscle, lose body fat, or find a meal plan to get lean, the goal is to develop eating habits you can maintain. You don’t need to copy every food on my plate. Use these examples to build meals that fit your preferences, support your training, and make consistency easier.

For a structured workout program with a day-by-day meal plan, check out the ATHLEAN-X website through the link above.

snippet.title: Do This AFTER Every Workout (NON NEGOTIABLE!)
snippet.description:
If there was one thing that I would recommend that everyone do at the end of every workout, it's a single exercise that serves a dual-purpose of not only building muscle, but protecting the shoulders as well. In this video, I am going to show you how the facepull is the perfect exercise to end your workouts with and why you should be doing it, regardless of what muscles you trained that day.

Fix Your Imbalances Here - https://athleanx.com
Subscribe To This Channel Here - http://bit.ly/2b0coMW

Too often do I see gym-goers focus solely on the front side of their bodies, not just with their aesthetics, but their health as well. The back side of the body is often neglected, simply because you cannot see it in the mirror. This leads to heavy imbalances, not just with muscular development, but with posture as well. When you focus all of your muscle building efforts on the front side of your body; yes you might create a well developed chest or arms, but at what cost?

When your muscle building efforts are directed to the front side off your body, you ignore the muscles that need to be strengthened in order to maintain proper biomechanical function and posture. More often than not, the muscles on the anterior side of the body are tight and the muscles on the backside are weak, unable to perform their proper functions.

The facepull fixes that, especially done at the end of every workout.

However, the face pull can be done with two purposes; hypertrophy and neuromuscular reeducation. Whether you treat this exercise as a muscle building effort or a corrective exercise, there is a very specific way for this face pull exercise to be done.

Instead of grabbing a standard rope, you want to use an extended rope (2 ft) or two standard ropes to perform the movement. This is because a single standard-sized rope won't allow you to get your arms wide enough to get the most out of the exercise. When you pull the rope towards your face, you should be able to create a 90 degree angle with your elbows. Think of it as performing a double front bicep pose. Getting your arms this wide allows for proper activation of the muscles and tendons of the rotator cuff

To properly achieve this position, you will need to grab the rope(s) with your thumbs up, contrary to the popular idea that your grab the rope(w) with an overhand grip. When your pull the rope(s) back toward you, your ending position should have your thumbs pointing back behind you.

The other key to this exercise is to prevent your shoulders from shrugging during the movement, especially when you pull the rope(s) towards you. The facepull is designed to build and strengthen the muscles that surround your shoulder and your upper back. We can continue doing this by either pausing for 2-3 seconds in the contracted position. We can further build upon this by performing an overhead trap raise like you see in the video. This will do a great job of neuromuscular reeducation and help to reset your upper back.

This will benefit not just muscle strength and size, but function as well. It will also help to correct your posture which has likely suffered from the high amounts of anterior focused training.

When it comes to when you are supposed to perform a facepull, either as a hypertrophy exercise or as a corrective exercise, it depends on your split. 2 days a week means one day for building muscle and one day for correction. 3 days, I prefer 2 corrective sessions compared to 1 muscle building session where they alternate (corrective / hypertrophy / corrective). 5 days a week, again, I want you to alternate with a greater focus on the neuromuscular reeducation. It would look this - corrective / hypertrophy / corrective / hypertrophy / corrective / corrective.

If you want to build muscle, fix your posture, or do both at the same time and think peptides are insane; then there really is no better exercise to get the job done than the facepull. There's a reason I've fallen in love with this exercise and I think that you would greatly benefit from including it in your training.

snippet.title: How to Do More Pullups in Your NEXT Set (GUARANTEED!)
snippet.description:
Want to do more pullups? Whether you can currently do 2 pullups, 5 pullups, 10 pullups or you're trying to reach 15, 20 or even 25 unbroken reps, the fastest way to increase pullups is not simply trying harder on every set. In this video, I’m going to show you exactly how to do more pullups by fixing six common mistakes that make every rep harder than it needs to be.

Do more pullups with programs here - https://athleanx.com
Subscribe To This Channel Here - http://bit.ly/2b0coMW

If you’ve been searching for how to increase pullups, how to get better at pullups, how to improve pullup strength or how to do more pullups in a row, this is where you want to start. Most people assume their problem is a lack of back strength. Sometimes it is. But very often the bigger issue is inefficient setup, wasted movement, poor body position and failing to use the strongest muscles possible to perform the exercise.

The first mistake is starting the pullup too loose. Hanging passively from the bar can create instability through the shoulders and shoulder blades, forcing you to waste energy before the rep even begins. Instead, engage the lats before you pull. Think about creating a slight backward angle rather than simply hanging straight down. This helps set the shoulder blades, turns on the lats and puts you in a much stronger position to initiate every rep.

Next, look at your elbows. If your elbows are directly in line with your body when viewed from the side, you may be missing a better pulling position. Getting the elbows slightly out in front places the shoulder closer to the scapular plane, gives the lats a better stretch and helps you produce more pulling strength while keeping the shoulder in a more comfortable position.

The third mistake might be the biggest reason you can’t do more pullups: energy leaks. If your legs are dangling, your knees are bent, your feet are crossed behind you and your body is moving around under the bar, you are making yourself feel heavier. Keep your legs together, knees straight, quads tight, glutes squeezed, core braced and feet slightly out in front. This creates one rigid line of force and can instantly make pullups feel easier.

Mistake number four is what you are doing with your hands. A shoulder-width grip is a strong starting point, but the real key is the direction of force. Instead of only thinking about pulling straight down on the bar, think about pulling down AND inward at the same time. Squeezing the hands toward each other while you pull can recruit more of the muscles that help adduct the arms and create a stronger, more stable pull.

The fifth mistake is attacking the bar with the wrong target. Stop thinking only about getting your chin over the bar. Instead, think about driving the upper sternum toward the bar. Reaching with the chest rather than collapsing forward with the chin helps keep your torso open, your back engaged and your line of pull more efficient. You do not have to touch your chest to the bar. The goal is to use the sternum as your target so you stay tight and powerful.

Finally, if you really want to know how to do more pullups, you have to stop treating pullups differently from every other strength exercise. Progressive overload matters. Just as you would add weight to a bench press to get stronger, weighted pullups can help build the strength needed to make bodyweight pullups easier. Add weight for lower-rep sets, then remove the weight and immediately perform bodyweight reps as a drop set. Over time, your weighted reps and bodyweight pullup numbers can climb together.

So if you have ever asked how to do more pullups, how to increase pullups fast, how to get better at pullups, how to improve pullup form, how to build pullup strength, how to increase pullup reps or how to do 20 pullups, start with these six corrections. Fix your setup. Engage the lats. Get the elbows in the right position. Eliminate energy leaks. Pull down and in. Lead with the sternum. Then add weighted pullups to progressively build strength.

The goal is simple: make every rep more efficient, then build the specific pulling strength needed to increase your pullup max.

Pullups are one of the best bodyweight exercises for building your back, lats, biceps, grip and upper body. The stronger and more technically sound you become, the easier it is to add reps and break through a pullup plateau.

snippet.title: STOP, You're Training Your Chest All Wrong!
snippet.description:
STOP, You’re Training Your Chest All Wrong. If your chest workout is built around doing the same traditional sets, resting two or three minutes, and then repeating them again, you may be wasting a lot of reps that aren’t doing nearly as much for muscle growth as you think.

Build a chiseled chest here - https://athleanx.com
Subscribe To This Channel Here - http://bit.ly/2b0coMW

In this video, I’m showing you a different way to train your chest using a hypertrophy technique called effective reps. The goal is simple: spend less time doing the easier reps that only get you to fatigue, and more time doing the hard, high-effort reps that are most responsible for stimulating new muscle growth.

To demonstrate how effective reps work, Jesse performs dumbbell bench press sets in two different styles. First, he performs a traditional set with a weight that causes failure somewhere around the 10 to 12 rep range. The first several reps are relatively easy. The real challenge doesn’t begin until the final reps, when effort rises sharply and every repetition becomes a grind.

Instead of resting two or three minutes and fully recovering before another traditional set, Jesse rests only about 15 to 30 seconds and gets right back into the dumbbell bench press. Because he has not fully recovered, he reaches those difficult reps almost immediately. Rather than spending another six or seven reps just trying to get back to the point where the set becomes hard, nearly every rep now demands a high level of effort.

This is a rest-pause style of training designed specifically for hypertrophy. It is not how I would train for maximal strength or power, where longer rest periods and high-quality reps are important. But if your goal is to build a bigger chest, increase muscle size, and make your chest workout more efficient, this technique gives you a new way to structure your sets.

The first set is what I call the ignition set. Choose a weight that makes you fail somewhere around 10 to 12 reps. That set gets you to the level of fatigue necessary to begin accumulating effective reps. After that, rest only 15 to 30 seconds, perform another set to failure, rest briefly again, and continue accumulating reps until you reach your target number.

For example, you might perform 20 effective reps on the dumbbell bench press. Your ignition set does not count toward those 20. After the short rest, you might get 5 effective reps, then 4, then 3, and continue chipping away until you reach 20 total effective reps. If your reps begin dropping to singles or doubles, reduce the weight slightly and continue.

This same strategy can be used to create an entire chest workout. You could perform 20 effective reps on the dumbbell bench press, move to an incline bench press to target the upper chest differently, then use cable crossovers, and finish with weighted or paused dips for another intense chest-building stimulus.

Instead of thinking only in terms of 3 sets of 10 or 4 sets of 12, you can begin programming your workout around the number of truly challenging reps you want to accumulate.

This can also help answer one of the most common questions lifters ask: how do I get a bigger chest when my current chest workout has stopped producing results? Sometimes the answer is not adding more exercises, more sets, or more total time in the gym. Sometimes it is changing the quality and effort of the reps you are already doing.

Effective reps require honest effort. If you stop a set too early, the entire method loses its purpose. With lighter weights and higher-rep sets, this becomes even more important because so many of the early repetitions are simply getting you closer to the reps that matter. If you choose a lighter weight, you still need to take the set close enough to true muscular failure for those final reps to become meaningful.

At the end of the video, you’ll also hear Josh Brolin and Chris DiStefano discussing this ATHLEAN-X effective reps approach on the Joe Rogan Experience. They talk about shortening the rest period, getting back into the hard reps faster, and how this style of training changed the way they think about building muscle.

If you have been searching for a new chest workout, a new way to build a bigger chest, how to get a bigger chest, how to build chest muscle faster, or how to make your dumbbell bench press more effective, try using effective reps and see how different your next workout feels.

Remember, building a bigger chest is not just about doing more work. It is about making more of your reps count.

snippet.title: STOP, You're Training Your Biceps All Wrong!
snippet.description:
If you want to know how to build bigger biceps, how to get bigger biceps, or how to build big biceps that look thicker from every angle, this video shows you why simply doing more curls may not be the answer. You can perform barbell curls, dumbbell curls, preacher curls, hammer curls and cable curls every week, but if the mechanics are wrong, you can still leave biceps growth on the table.

Get the exact workouts and programs used by physical therapist Jeff Cavaliere here - https://athleanx.com
Subscribe To This Channel Here - http://bit.ly/2b0coMW

The biceps are not just elbow flexors. The biceps brachii also plays an important role in supinating the forearm, which means turning the palm upward. If you ignore that function and simply move a weight from the bottom of a curl to the top, you may be completing the rep without getting everything you can out of the muscle you are trying to build.

In this video, I break down the most common biceps training mistakes that can keep your arms from growing and show you how to fix the way you perform your curls.

One of the biggest mistakes is allowing other muscles to dominate the curl. When the shoulders drift forward, the elbows travel too far, the wrists bend excessively or momentum starts swinging the weight, the biceps can lose the tension you thought you were creating. Heavy curls are not automatically bad, but using more weight only helps if the target muscle is still doing the work.

Whether you are doing a barbell curl or dumbbell curl, think beyond simply getting the weight to your shoulders. Keep the tension where it belongs, control the eccentric on the way down, and use a range of motion that lets you challenge the biceps without turning the movement into a full-body exercise.

Supination is another major piece of building bigger biceps. If you are using dumbbells, actively turn the palm up as you raise the weight and continue trying to supinate near the top. This helps you train one of the true functions of the biceps instead of treating every curl like nothing more than elbow flexion.

Grip position can also change what you feel. A hammer curl is a great arm exercise, but it shifts more emphasis toward the brachialis and brachioradialis because the forearm stays in a neutral position. Those muscles matter for bigger arms, but if your goal is maximum biceps development, you still need curls that allow you to aggressively supinate the forearm.

Shoulder position matters too. The long head of the biceps crosses the shoulder joint, so where your upper arm sits changes the position of the muscle. Incline dumbbell curls challenge the biceps with the arm behind the body, while other curl variations place the arm more in front of the torso. A complete biceps workout should not rely on one curl angle forever.

You also want to stop ignoring the eccentric portion of your biceps exercises. It is easy to focus entirely on curling the weight up and then let it fall back down. Instead, control the lowering portion of every rep. The negative is another opportunity to keep tension on the biceps and make the set more productive.

Progressive overload matters, but overload is only useful when you are progressively overloading the muscle you intended to train. If every increase in weight causes more hip drive, shoulder movement and swinging, you may be getting better at moving the weight without getting better at training your biceps.

This is especially important if your biceps are not growing despite plenty of arm training. Before adding more sets of curls, look at how you are performing the sets you already have. Better biceps training often comes from better execution, exercise selection, stronger supination, controlled eccentrics and keeping tension on the biceps through the rep.

The takeaway is simple: stop judging a biceps exercise only by how much weight you can curl. Judge it by how effectively you can load the biceps, maintain tension, use the functions of the muscle and progressively challenge those mechanics over time. When you clean up your curl form, the same exercises can suddenly feel completely different.

If your biceps have stopped growing, your arms look flat from the front, or you simply want to know the best way to build bigger biceps, start with the fixes shown in this video. You do not necessarily need more biceps exercises. You need to get more out of the right ones.

snippet.title: STOP, You're Training Your Triceps All Wrong!
snippet.description:
If you want to know how to build bigger triceps, how to get bigger triceps, or how to build big triceps that fill out your shirt sleeves, this video shows you what you may be missing. You can do tricep pushdowns, close grip bench presses, skull crushers, overhead extensions and kickbacks, but if you are not putting the long head of the triceps under tension in the right positions, your arms can still look flat from the side and lack the thickness you are after.

Fix Flat Triceps Here - http://athleanx.com/x/fix-flat-triceps
Subscribe To This Channel Here - http://bit.ly/2b0coMW

The long head is the largest head of the triceps and one of the biggest contributors to overall upper arm size. If your goal is to build bigger arms, you cannot just add more tricep exercises. You have to challenge the long head in both positions where it can work hardest: with the arm overhead in shoulder flexion to create a strong stretch, and with the arm driven back behind the body into shoulder extension to create a hard shortened-position contraction.

In this video, I break down the most common triceps training mistakes that keep people from getting bigger triceps and show you how to fix each one.

First, we look at the skull crusher. Most people lower the weight toward the forehead and think they are maximizing the stretch on the long head. The problem is that the upper arm often stays too far in front of the body. By allowing the arms to angle farther back behind the head and then keeping that upper-arm position fixed while bending and straightening the elbows, you can place much more tension on the long head of the triceps.

Next is the tricep push away. This exercise can be great for building big triceps, but only if the line of pull is right. If the arms finish too low and become almost parallel to the rope, tension drops. The fix is to finish with the arms higher so the forearms stay more perpendicular to the cable. I also show you the step-through push away, which lets you use more weight, create controlled momentum on the concentric, and then overload the eccentric while still getting a strong overhead stretch.

The third exercise is the dumbbell overhead tricep extension, or power bomb. This is one of the most popular exercises for anyone trying to get bigger triceps, but shoulder mobility and elbow position can ruin it. When the elbows flare wide, elbow range of motion gets shorter and the triceps lose tension. By setting an incline bench behind you, you can reduce the shoulder-flexion demand, keep the elbows more forward and close to the head, and still get a deep stretch on the triceps without forcing the shoulders into an uncomfortable position.

Stretch-focused tricep exercises matter, but they are not the only exercises that matter. To fully develop the long head, you also need movements that take the arm behind the body and place the triceps in a strongly shortened position.

That is where the Wolverine pulldown comes in. Because the long head crosses the shoulder joint, it also helps extend the arm behind the body. The Wolverine pulldown combines a pulling motion with elbow extension, allowing you to pull the elbows tight to the body and then drive the hands behind you for an intense contraction. This complements your overhead work and helps create more complete triceps development.

Finally, we fix the dumbbell tricep kickback. Kickbacks get criticized because they are often done badly. As fatigue sets in, the lower back rounds, the elbows drop, and the exercise becomes a weak elbow extension. The solution is to perform the kickback face down on an incline bench. The bench stabilizes your torso, removes the low-back limitation, and lets you deliberately drag the elbows behind the body before extending the dumbbells. This ensures every rep starts from the position that maximizes contraction of the long head.

If your triceps look flat, your arms do not fill your sleeves, or you feel like your triceps have stopped growing even though you train them consistently, this video will show you how to build bigger triceps by improving exercise selection, setup, range of motion, arm position and tension instead of simply doing more sets.

The biggest takeaway is simple: if you want to know how to get bigger triceps, train the long head in both a stretched position and a fully shortened position. Combine both and you give yourself a better chance to build thicker, fuller triceps.

snippet.title: 5 Bodyweight Exercises That Fix 95% Of Your Problems
snippet.description:
22 Days to More Pullups - https://athleanx.com/morepullups
Subscribe to this channel here - http://bit.ly/2b0coMW

If you are looking for 5 exercises that fix 95% of your problems, then you’ve come to the right place. In this video, I am going to show you 5 different exercises that will help to deal with the common problem areas in the body as well as working on those stiff and achey joints so you can feel loose and pain free throughout the day.

The first exercise up a pushup variation done to target very specific problem areas. If you have bad posture, rounded, tight, achey shoulders and low back problems, this hand-release superman pushup will address those areas immediately. By extending the arms straight out in front, you are promoting overhead shoulder biomechanics and thoracic extension. When it comes to bad posture, we often have trouble getting our arms overhead, especially due to rounding of the thoracic spine. If we can get thoracic extension, we can promote good posture. It's important to note that we often neglect the muscles on the backside of our body, which leads to weakness which then leads to poor posture and biomechanics. 

When it comes to addressing the lower back, we often have a weakness in the lumbar spine area. We focus most of our efforts on building size and strength of the lats, but the muscles of the lower back, when weak, can become painful. By lifting our legs off the ground in this superman pushup, we are directly strengthening the muscles of the low back.

The second exercise that will fix 95% of your body's problems is a combination between one of my favorite mobility exercises and one of my favorite ab exercises. The bridge and reach over will again promote thoracic mobility, helping to alleviate some of the postural problems you may have. On top of that, though, this part of the combo will also help to strengthen the glutes. Weak glutes often contributes to dysfunction like anterior pelvic tilt and low back pain. Therefore, if we can strengthen the glutes while working on the posture of our upper body, we will be setting ourselves up for postural success and a life without chronic pain.

The second half of this combo features the heels to the heaven exercise or swiper. Swiping your hands underneath your low back while you perform this exercise will give immediate feedback that you are doing the movement correctly. If you can't swipe your hands underneath, you are not getting your pelvis off the ground. This means that you are likely using your hip flexors instead of your lower abs to initiate the movement.

The third exercise that you should be doing in an effort to fix 95% of your problems is another combination that mashes up a bodyweight squat and static reverse creeping lunge. Here we will again address thoracic extension as you will need to stay as upright as possible during the entire movement. This can be reinforced by folding your hands and holding them against your sternum - your knuckles should be facing the ceiling at all times. Squat down and pause, from here, step back one leg into a reverse lunge, return and step back the other leg.

This combo is extremely effective at targeting hip stability because of the unilateral nature of the lunge portion of the exercise. Stronger hips will lead to better balance as well as preventing back pain. Most sources of low back pain don't come from your back directly, but weakness in the muscles of the hips like the glute medius.

The next exercise is a home variation on one of my favorite exercises that I find to be extremely beneficial when it comes to training the upper body and correcting any deficiencies we may have. The doorway facepull. Simply press against the door frame with the back of your hands and pull your upper body forward until you feel the muscles in your upper back and rear delts engaging.

This exercise will strengthen the muscles of the upper back that often get neglected, along with the rear delts and the rotator cuff (thanks to the external rotation present within the exercises form itself). snippet.title: You Hate Your Saggy Chest (HERE'S HOW TO FIX IT!)
snippet.description:
Build a Muscular Chest Here - https://athleanx.com
Subscribe to This Channel Here - https://bit.ly/2b0coMW

If your chest won’t grow no matter how much you bench press, this video explains the REAL reason your pecs may not be responding and what you can do to finally build a bigger chest. I’m breaking down chest growth, pec activation, bench press technique, chest genetics, dips, pushups, cable presses, fly variations and the mistakes that can keep your shoulders doing the work instead of your chest.

A lot of guys assume a lagging chest simply needs more weight, more exercises or more volume. But if you’ve been consistently bench pressing for a long time and your pecs still aren’t growing, the problem may not be effort. It may be that your chest is never becoming the dominant muscle in the exercises you’re using.

The bench press should absolutely be a foundational chest exercise. If you haven’t been bench pressing consistently for at least a year, you may simply need more time building strength and improving your technique.

For many lifters, the anterior delts and triceps dominate pressing movements. You may be moving impressive weight without creating enough tension in the pecs. That’s why chest adduction exercises can be so important.

Exercises that bring the arm across the body can help you learn how to contract the pecs more effectively and carry that chest activation into your pressing exercises.

Cable crossovers and cable flys are great options. If you don’t have a cable machine, a dumbbell floor fly can be a useful alternative. I prefer the floor fly to a traditional dumbbell bench fly because the floor limits the bottom range and can reduce the vulnerable position of the shoulder.

But activation is only part of the story.

At some point, chest genetics and skeletal structure matter too. The width and length of your clavicles and your overall frame influence how much total muscle mass your chest can visually carry. That doesn’t mean you should blame genetics. Different lifters simply have different ceilings and chest shapes.

The goal is to maximize YOUR pec development by building the lower chest line, improving thickness through the middle pecs and developing the upper chest so you create that fuller shelf near the clavicles. 

You do this by training the chest with intent instead of treating every chest exercise like a strength test.

One major change is to separate strength training from hypertrophy focused chest training.

Let the barbell bench press be a strength exercise if that’s where you perform best. Then use other chest exercises with lighter weights, slower reps and more control to make the pecs do the work.

On a dumbbell bench press, try pausing at the bottom of each rep. Keep the shoulders back and think about initiating the press with the chest instead of simply driving the dumbbells upward. That brief pause can help eliminate momentum and force you to create tension with the muscle you’re trying to grow.

The same idea applies to dips.

Dips can be an excellent lower chest exercise, but only if you perform them correctly. If your shoulders roll forward as you press up, you may be shifting stress away from the pecs while putting the shoulders in a less favorable position. Slow the movement down, maintain control and initiate the rep with the chest.

Another excellent option is the cable bench press. This doesn’t replace the regular bench press. Instead, the cables pull slightly outward, forcing the pecs to contribute more strongly through their adduction function. For someone who struggles to feel their chest, this can be a game changer.

And if you train at home with no equipment, you can still improve chest activation with pushups.

Slow the pushup down. Don’t just think about pushing your body away from the floor. Think about lifting your sternum as you press and squeezing the pecs to move your torso upward. That can make a pushup feel completely different.

If your chest won’t grow, don’t automatically assume you need more weight, more sets or more exercises. 

First make sure your pecs are contributing the way they should. Improve your mind-muscle connection, control the eccentric, slow down your reps, use exercises that reinforce horizontal adduction and stop letting the shoulders dominate every press.

If you’re looking to build a bigger chest, increase pec activation, improve your bench press technique, grow your upper chest, build your lower chest or finally fix a stubborn chest that refuses to grow, these principles will give you a much better path forward.

For complete ATHLEAN-X training programs designed to build muscle and increase strength, visit athleanx.com at the link above.

If your LOWER CHEST is the problem, watch the Lower Chest Solution next.

If your UPPER CHEST won’t grow, watch the Upper Chest Solution next.

snippet.title: 7 Exercises That Are Making Your Shoulder WORSE
snippet.description:
Train Without Pain Here - https://athleanx.com
Subscribe to This Channel Here - https://bit.ly/2b0coMW

If you have any kind of a shoulder pain, you're probably looking for the 7 most troublesome exercises for a bum shoulder. In this video, I am going to go over what those 7 troublesome exercises are if you are dealing with a bad shoulder (or shoulders for that manner). Not only that, but I am going to show you how to manage those exercises so that you can keep training and getting gains without the pains.

When it comes to working out with shoulder pain, I know that there are 7 exercises that are troublesome. Does that mean you should stop doing them altogether? Or is there something that can be done to mitigate the pain while still getting the benefits of the exercise? As a physical therapist and someone that has bad shoulders myself, I can tell you that avoiding these exercises altogether is not the solution.

The first exercise that could be a problem with shoulder pain is one you might not immediately think of and that's the pullup. In the case of a labrum tear, this can be one of the most aggravating exercises. The fix here is to depress your shoulders - create distance between your ears and your biceps as you hang from the bar. When you are lowering yourself down from the top of the pull-up, there are 2 things you need to do. The first is to slow yourself down as you descend. The second is to never disengage the packing of your shoulders throughout the rep. This will let you keep getting the benefits of the pullup without aggravating a compromised labrum.

The next troublesome exercise for a bum shoulder is an obvious one that, again, you shouldn't be skipping. That is the bench press. Most people experience shoulder pain or shoulder discomfort on the bench press when they use a barbell. That is because of the fixed arm position of the arms when using the bar. If you are going to use a barbell to bench press, then you will want to take a more narrow grip. This will help with elbow positioning in preventing you from flaring your arms out to the sides (incurring greater internal rotation) as well as activating the lats to stabilize the press. In many cases, I would say that if a barbell bench press is causing shoulder pain, then you're likely better off switching to dumbbells. This will allow freedom to tuck the elbows as much as needed to avoid shoulder pain. The key here is to go slow to create greater stability.

If there is one exercise you should skip altogether when it comes to working out with shoulder pain, it would be the upright row. It's just not a good exercise due to its ability to create shoulder problems in the first place (such as with impingement) and any benefits it has when it comes to shoulder growth can be mirrored by another, safer exercise. In this instance, simply opt to perform a dumbbell high pull instead. The added benefit of external rotation at the top of the rep will help prevent impingement and promote healthy shoulder mechanics.

We don't only have to focus on the upper body to find exercises that will be tough on a creaky shoulder. As a matter of fact, the king of leg exercises, the squat, can be a big problem if you don't have the right shoulder mobility. I'm specifically talking about the low bar squat, which requires a lot of shoulder external rotation to get into the proper position. However, we have some simple fixes so you can still squat without pain. If low bar squatting is what you want to do, try a wider grip for less shoulder mobility demand. Otherwise, you can switch to a high bar squat or a front squat, which will still have a heavy impact on your leg growth.

Now, I've heard time and time again that if you have bad shoulders, you shouldn't do dips. I disagree. I think you just need to pay attention to how you are performing the exercise. The first thing to take note of is that you should be taking the same tip from the pullups when it comes to depressing your shoulder blades - keep your shoulders back and down throughout the entire movement. On top of that, stick your chest out. A proud chest will make sure your chest is taking the brunt of the work instead of the shoulders. Don't think you need some extreme amount of stretch at the bottom of the rep either. Cut your depth a little short to where you are getting some stretch on the pecs without aggravating your shoulder pain.

Finish watching the video to the very end to see the rest of the 7 most troublesome exercises for a bum shoulder.
